content: Parent-infant psychotherapy (PIP) is a therapeutic intervention designed to address the relationship between a parent and their infant. It involves working with both the parent and the infant together, aiming to enhance the quality of their relationship, foster secure attachment in the infant, and support the infant's optimal development. This approach focuses on the parent's perception of their infant, which may be influenced by the parent's own past experiences, and seeks to connect these perceptions to the current parent-child relationship to directly improve their bond. The primary objectives of this review were to evaluate the effectiveness of PIP in improving mental health outcomes for both parents and infants, as well as the quality of the parent-infant relationship. Additionally, the review aimed to identify specific components of PIP programs that contribute to better outcomes and to explore factors that may influence the effectiveness of the intervention, such as the duration or focus of the program. To gather relevant data, a comprehensive search of multiple electronic databases was conducted on January 13, 2014. These databases included the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), Ovid MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, PsycINFO, BIOSIS Citation Index, Science Citation Index, ERIC, and Sociological Abstracts. Additional sources, such as trial registries, reference lists, and direct contact with study authors and experts, were also utilized. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-randomized controlled trials (quasi-RCTs) that compared PIP programs targeting parents with infants aged 24 months or younger to control conditions (e.g., waiting lists, no treatment, or treatment-as-usual). Studies were required to use at least one standardized measure of parental or infant functioning. Some studies also included comparisons with alternative treatment groups. The methodological quality of the included studies was assessed using standard Cochrane Collaboration procedures. Treatment effects were standardized by calculating the mean difference (MD) in post-intervention scores between intervention and control groups, divided by the pooled standard deviation. Results were presented as standardized mean differences (SMDs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for continuous data and risk ratios (RRs) for dichotomous data. Meta-analyses were conducted using a random-effects model. The review included eight studies with a total of 846 randomized participants. Four studies compared PIP to control groups, while the other four compared PIP to alternative treatments (e.g., video-interaction guidance, psychoeducation, counseling, or cognitive behavioral therapy). Some studies included high-risk populations, such as mothers with postpartum depression, insecure attachment, or a history of maltreatment, as well as incarcerated mothers. The risk of bias was assessed across several domains, including random sequence generation, allocation concealment, incomplete outcome data, selective reporting, blinding of participants and personnel, and blinding of outcome assessment. Four studies were judged to have a low risk of bias in four or more domains, while four studies had a high risk of bias for allocation concealment. None of the studies blinded participants or personnel to the intervention, and five studies provided insufficient information to assess bias in at least one domain. Six studies contributed data to comparisons between PIP and control groups, resulting in 19 meta-analyses of outcomes measured at post-intervention or follow-up. Primary outcomes included parental depression (both dichotomous and continuous measures), parent-child interaction (e.g., maternal sensitivity, child involvement, and parent engagement), infant attachment categories (secure, avoidant, disorganized, resistant), attachment changes (e.g., insecure to secure), infant behavior, and secondary outcomes such as infant cognitive development. The results showed no significant differences between PIP and control groups for parental depression, either in terms of incidence (RR 0.74, 95% CI 0.52 to 1.04; 3 studies, 278 participants; low-quality evidence) or parent-reported levels of depression (SMD -0.22, 95% CI -0.46 to 0.02; 4 studies, 356 participants; low-quality evidence). However, there were some improvements favoring PIP in infant attachment outcomes. Specifically, PIP was associated with a higher proportion of securely attached infants at post-intervention (RR 8.93, 95% CI 1.25 to 63.70; 2 studies, 168 participants; very low-quality evidence), fewer infants with avoidant attachment (RR 0.48, 95% CI 0.24 to 0.95; 2 studies, 168 participants; low-quality evidence), fewer infants with disorganized attachment (RR 0.32, 95% CI 0.17 to 0.58; 2 studies, 168 participants; low-quality evidence), and a greater proportion of infants transitioning from insecure to secure attachment (RR 11.45, 95% CI 3.11 to 42.08; 2 studies, 168 participants; low-quality evidence). No significant differences were observed between PIP and control groups for other primary outcomes, such as adverse effects, or for secondary outcomes. Similarly, comparisons between PIP and alternative treatments did not reveal significant differences in outcomes related to parental mental health, parent-infant interaction, infant attachment, infant behavior, or cognitive development. The quality of the evidence was rated as low or very low for most outcomes, including parental depression and infant attachment security. The evidence was downgraded due to risks of bias in study design and execution, small sample sizes, wide confidence intervals (indicating imprecision), and, in some cases, clinical and statistical heterogeneity (indicating inconsistency). These limitations reduced confidence in the estimated effects of PIP. In conclusion, while PIP shows promise in improving infant attachment security in high-risk families, there is no strong evidence to suggest that it is more effective than no treatment, treatment-as-usual, or alternative interventions for other parentor relationship-based outcomes. Further high-quality research is needed to determine the impact of PIP on key mediating factors, such as parental mental health, reflective functioning, and parent-infant interaction.
